text: Quick question. Your heart beats a hundred thousand times a day. It never stops. It never rests. So how is it built to do that? Let's zoom in and find out.
First, where is it? Right here. In the middle of your chest. Between your two lungs. Tilted a little to the left. And about the size of your fist.

Now let's zoom in to the wall. It has three layers. Outside, the epicardium. In the middle, the thick muscle, the myocardium. That's the part that pumps. And inside, a smooth lining, the endocardium. The whole heart sits in a protective bag, the pericardium.

Now let's cut the heart open. Here's the big idea. The heart is really two pumps, side by side. The right pump sends blood to the lungs. The left pump sends blood to the whole body. A wall, the septum, keeps them apart.
Each pump has two rooms. Upstairs, the atrium. It receives blood. Downstairs, the ventricle. It pumps blood out. So, four chambers in total.
Now look closely at the walls. See how the left ventricle is much thicker? It's the bodybuilder of the heart. It has to push blood all the way to your toes. Exam tip: thickest wall, left ventricle.
Blood must only go one way. So the heart has four one way doors: the valves. Here's a trick to remember them in order. Try Pulling My Aorta. Tricuspid. Pulmonary. Mitral. Aortic.

Let's zoom into the tricuspid valve. See these thin strings? They're the chordae tendineae, tied to small papillary muscles. Like the strings of a parachute, they stop the valve from flipping backward.
Now pull back. Big vessels connect the heart. The vena cava brings blood in. The pulmonary trunk goes to the lungs. The pulmonary veins come back. And the aorta, the biggest artery, goes to the body.
So remember three things. Two pumps. Four chambers. Four one way doors. Next time: how all these parts work together.
